about: The steps of the turret build video (second take, CAD-style UI + pin-level wiring), in order: what the agent (Claude) sent through napl.design.viewer.Backend (the object the viewer window talks to) while building assemblies/turret.toml, pins included, from an empty design. `reqs` are Backend requests (tool + args; `wait` = seconds to let the window show it; `until` = wait for the window to commit an animated drop; `expect_fail` = the Design is expected to refuse it); `macro: place` = LIBRARY page search typed into the box, then an animated library.drag from the part's card to its port (the window flies the ghost and sends the drop itself), then the step's `post` requests (selection, camera orbit). `why` is the agent's reason, shown as the caption. tools/record_turret.py replays this file.

steps.title: Start from an empty design: the base plate
steps.why: Nothing is placed yet. I search the library for the plate that carries the servo, compute and launcher mounts: the project's own machined turret base plate. It becomes the root, the frame everything else is mated to.

steps.title: A turret is bolted down: fixed base, 1 ms step
steps.why: A new design starts as a free-floating vehicle. This is a turret on a mast, so the base is fixed (the root is welded to the world) and the physics step is 1 ms; the plate drops from its floor lift to the origin.

ops.description: Counter-UAS demo turret: pan-tilt (2 x XL430-W250-T) with a generic .177 pellet launcher, Pi Camera Module 3 and Raspberry Pi 5

steps.title: Filter the library: 12 V servos
steps.why: The two axes need bus servos on the 12 V supply with torque to turn a 0.3 kg launcher. Category motor.servo plus a numeric filter v_nominal 11-13 V leaves the 12 V ones; I narrow the text to 'xl430'.

steps.title: Pan servo onto the plate's servo seat
steps.why: Dynamixel XL430-W250-T: 1.5 N*m stall, 12 V, TTL bus, in stock in the library with datasheet numbers. Dropped on the plate, it snaps to the servo_seat port (bolt pattern and clearance decide the placement). The browser tree on the left gains the part; PROPERTIES shows it.

steps.title: Yoke on the pan servo's horn, as a hinge
steps.why: The yoke turns with the horn: mating it to pan.output with a hinge joint makes the pan axis. The range is a design limit just inside a full turn, so the cable run is not wound up.

range.rationale: Design limit just inside a full turn so the cable run is not wound up; the XL430 itself turns freely (position mode covers one revolution of the encoder).

steps.title: Tilt servo in the yoke
steps.why: A second XL430 for the tilt axis, snapped into the yoke's servo seat: the same part, a second instance with its own bus ID.

steps.title: Bus IDs: pan 1, tilt 2
steps.why: Two servos on one TTL bus need distinct IDs. A bare number is refused by the numbers rule, so each carries its unit, fidelity and rationale.

value.rationale: Bus ID chosen by the builder: pan 1, tilt 2.
Bus ID chosen by the builder: pan 1, tilt 2.

steps.title: Launcher on the tilt horn (reversed hinge)
steps.why: A generic .177 pneumatic pellet launcher (air-rifle class, point-mass ballistics). Mated to tilt.output; the servo's positive direction lowers it, so the hinge is reversed: positive tilt raises the muzzle.

range.rationale: Design limits: 20 deg depression to 77 deg elevation (the launcher's action box meets the turntable below about -20 deg).

steps.title: Camera on the launcher's camera seat
steps.why: A Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 (41 deg vertical field of view) co-aligned with the barrel: when the camera centres a drone, the barrel points at it. It rides the tilt axis.

steps.title: Raspberry Pi 5 on the compute seat
steps.why: The tracker runs on a Pi 5. It snaps onto the plate's compute_seat (no extra screws: the standoff studs will hold it); four standoffs go under it next, because the seat plane is 14 mm above the plate.

steps.title: Mass of the Pi: not published, so an estimate
steps.why: The Pi 5 product brief gives no mass. A bare board weighs about 46 g; I record that as an estimate with the reason, so the mass budget says where the number came from.

value.rationale: The Raspberry Pi 5 product brief publishes no mass; a bare Pi 5 board weighs about 45-50 g, 46 g taken. Only its inertia on the base plate depends on it.

steps.title: Standoff 1 of 4 (M2.5 brass, 14 mm)
steps.why: The Pi's four mounting holes need standoffs. I switch port snapping off (these are free posts, not a mated stack) and drag the first one onto the plate near its hole; exact coordinates come afterwards.

steps.title: Standoffs 2 to 4
steps.why: Same part, three more drops around the rectangle of holes (58 x 49 mm pattern). Rough positions only; the next step tidies them.

steps.title: Ribbon tools: Move with edge snapping and guide lines, Align
steps.why: The ribbon's Move tool with edge snapping: the second standoff's edge snaps to the first one's and a guide line shows the match. Then Align puts the rear pair on one x.

steps.title: Exact hole coordinates
steps.why: From the Pi 5 mechanical drawing the holes sit 58 mm apart across and 49 mm along, 85 mm board. I type the four positions in the PROPERTIES panel, which is a gizmo move to an exact point (metres, world frame).

steps.title: Rotate tool, then undo
steps.why: I try the Rotate tool on a standoff to see the angle snap (15 degree steps). It is a round post, so the turn changes nothing useful; one Undo takes it back (the HISTORY panel lists it).

steps.title: Browser tree eye: hide the Pi to see the four standoffs
steps.why: The eye next to a part in the BROWSER hides it in the 3D view (view only, the design is unchanged). With the Pi hidden the four standoffs stand in the 58 x 49 mm hole pattern; MEASURE reads the distance between two of them. Then the Pi comes back.

steps.title: Colours
steps.why: Colours are cosmetic and saved with the design: the yoke orange, the base plate dark grey, the launcher black and the camera bright, so the sub-assemblies read at a glance.

steps.title: Bench parts: the supplies, the servo adapter, the pellet
steps.why: Parts that stay off the turret (12 V and 5 V supplies, the Waveshare servo adapter, two cables, the pellet) are added as off-board instances. They carry the electrical wiring and the ammunition data, but no body.

steps.title: The DRC says what is still open
steps.why: Mechanics are done; the status bar and the DRC panel list the power ports nobody has wired. That is the next job: the 2D wiring sheet. View cube first: Front, Top and back to the home view.

steps.title: Pick the components of the 12 V servo chain
steps.why: WIRING workspace, first sheet: the 12 V supply, the servo adapter and the two servos. The sheet shows the real connectors of each part (DC jack, 3-pin servo bus, TTL plugs), not a simplified box.

steps.title: Flatten to the schematic sheet
steps.why: flatten: one card per component, sources left, loads right, each connector with its numbered pins taken from the part's datasheet pin table.

steps.title: Autowire says no: unlike connectors
steps.why: I drag the adapter's servo bus to the pan servo and let autowire choose the lead. It refuses, with the reason: the connector families differ. A deliberate bridge needs a wire part I choose myself.

steps.title: The 12 V net and the servo chain, pin to pin
steps.why: Supply cord into the adapter's DC jack (DC+ and DC-, the cord belongs to the supply), adapter to the pan servo with an AWG 22 silicone lead on GND / VCC / SIG, and the Dynamixel cable from pan to tilt for the daisy chain. Routed wires around the cards, gauge labels.

length.rationale: Not published. The adapter sits beside the base plate: 0.15 m, as the SO-101 and Koch board-to-servo leads.

steps.title: Second sheet: the Raspberry Pi 5 with its real connectors
steps.why: The Pi, its own 5 V supply, the adapter's UART pads and the camera. The Pi keeps its full connectors: the 2 x 20 GPIO header J8, the USB-C power input and the 22-pin camera FPC, every pin with its number and function straight from the datasheet. This is the full wiring, not a simplified box.

steps.title: The Pi's 5 V supply into its USB-C power pins
steps.why: The Pi gets its own 5 V 4 A supply through a bare 0.5 m lead onto VBUS (A4) and GND (A1) of its USB-C power connector (the library has no USB-C PD source, so it is a bridge of unlike connectors, with the estimate recorded).

length.rationale: Not published; a short lead from a bench supply beside the base plate.

steps.title: Zoom in on the Pi's GPIO header: all 40 pins readable
steps.why: At 100 % every pin shows its number and GPIO name (alternate functions in the tooltip). The sheet pans up the header: pin 6 is ground, pin 8 GPIO14 (UART0 TX), pin 10 GPIO15 (UART0 RX).

steps.title: UART to the servo adapter: first try, TX to TXD
steps.why: 3.3 V UART0 from the Pi's header to the adapter's UART pads. My first try joins Pi TX (pin 8) to the adapter's TXD and Pi RX (pin 10) to its RXD, straight through.

length.rationale: Not published. Pi header to adapter UART pads across the base plate, about 0.25 m of hook-up wire.

steps.title: The pin DRC catches it, with the reason
steps.why: Both conductors are flagged on the sheet and in the DRC: GPIO14 has no RX function and GPIO15 no TX function, so TX would face TX. The wire is removed.

steps.title: Fixed: UART crossed, TX to RXD, RX to TXD, plus ground
steps.why: TX goes to the adapter's RXD, RX to its TXD, pin 6 to GND: three conductors, 26 AWG hook-up wire. The DRC is clean again. The lead's few grams are not in the mass budget (included in the Pi), so the turret's mass stays what the simulation was run with.

length.rationale: Not published. Pi header to adapter UART pads across the base plate, about 0.25 m of hook-up wire.

steps.title: The camera ribbon: 15 conductors into the Pi's 22-pin CAM0
steps.why: The Camera Module 3's 15-pin FPC goes to the Pi 5's 22-pin CAM/DISP 0 connector: the cable adapts 15 to 22 pins, so pins 1-10 and 17, 18, 20, 21, 22 carry the data lanes, clock, I2C and 3.3 V. One conductor per strand on the sheet.

length.rationale: Camera Module 3 ships a 200 mm ribbon (S1 of raspberry-pi-camera-module-3); the Pi 5 end adapts 15 to 22 pins.

steps.title: Back to 3D: the wires are tubes routed around the parts
steps.why: The wires are already in the design. Back in the 3D view each conductor is a tube with the diameter of its gauge, leaving its connector along the connector axis and routed around the parts (a distance field of the assembly, A* through the free space), not through them.

steps.title: Close orbit: the camera ribbon and the UART leads clear the parts
steps.why: Close in on the Pi and the camera: the 15-conductor ribbon runs from the camera board around the launcher body to the Pi's CAM0 socket and the UART conductors leave the header upright, none of them crosses a solid. The camera moves around and below them.

steps.title: One more orbit around the pan-tilt stack
steps.why: A last full circle at mid distance, then back to the overview: the ribbon leaves the camera board, passes over the launcher body and the yoke and drops to the Pi without touching a solid.

steps.title: Device bindings: the simulation side
steps.why: The simulator needs to know what each part does: supplies, the wire adapter, the two servos (with the XL430 parameter map), the launcher with its pellet, the camera. Values come from part data through the maps; the thermal terms are estimates with a reason.

resistance.rationale: As assemblies/koch.toml: the part publishes no series resistance; 20 mohm = the DC jack contact pair plus a short trace, and a zero-resistance edge would be singular.

motor.c_th.rationale: No published winding thermal capacity for the XL430; 10 J/K as assemblies/koch.toml (same servo).

width.rationale: Program frame size: 1280 x 720 has the sensor's 16:9 aspect (4608 x 2592), so the field of view is used whole; chosen for the tracker's compute budget, not a sensor mode of record.

rate_hz.rationale: Program frame rate: the tracker's compute budget, not a sensor mode of record.

steps.title: The design as text, then the programs
steps.why: PROGRAM workspace: the design as TOML (every number with its source), then the turret program turret.py: camera pixels in, pan / tilt goals out, fire only after the operator authorizes.

steps.title: The drones' pseudorandom swarm program
steps.why: swarm.py: seeded boids (separation, cohesion, alignment, a random-walk wander) steered inside an arena in front of the turret. Same seed, same flight: the run is deterministic and replays exactly.

steps.title: The scenario file
steps.why: cuas.scenario.toml: what to run (scene + turret.py), the limits, and six monitors the runner judges on the trace: no shot without authorization, at least 3 drones engaged, at least 1 destroyed.

steps.title: Save the design
steps.why: Design.save writes the assembly as TOML, pins included. This file is what the simulation flies next: the turret above, not a copy of the reference.
